passage: The Class 5 group had one rule on the back bench: nobody says no yet. Maria held the smudged notebook while Pema called out ideas, and the others followed. A talking crow. A lost tiffin box. A king who hates mangoes. Nobody laughed at the strange ones, and by the time the bell rang for lunch the page held twenty lines. After the break they read the list again. Anything needing a real boat or a cart full of props got a line drawn through it, since the stage was small. Maria counted what was left and circled three: the crow, the tiffin box and the mango king. They would try each one out on Friday.

qa.q: How many lines did the page hold when the bell rang for lunch?
qa.a: The page held twenty lines when the bell rang for lunch.

qa.q: What was Pema probably feeling while calling out the strange ideas?
qa.a: Pema was probably feeling free and excited, since nobody laughed and the ideas kept coming.

qa.q: What other way could the group pick their final three, and why might it work?
qa.a: After the cutting, each child could put a small tick beside a favourite, which gives everyone a say while the small stage still limits the choice.

qa.q: How might a classmate whose boat idea was crossed out see this plan?
qa.a: They might feel a little let down at first, but could accept it because every idea was written down and the reason was the small stage.

grounding: Shows a group listing many ideas first, then removing those that need too many props and keeping three.

passage:
"Rule one," Kashish said, holding the marker. "No arguing. Every idea goes on the chart. Even silly ones."
"A lost puppy," Francis said.
Kashish wrote it. "Next."
"A ghost in the library." "A robot teacher." "Two kings fighting over a mango." "Aliens at the school sports day." The ideas kept coming until the chart paper had twenty.
"Now we judge," Kashish said. "Which ones need too many props?"
"The robot teacher needs a costume."
"Aliens need spaceships."
"Kings need crowns and a throne."
They crossed out eleven. Then five more that needed too many actors.
"Four left," Francis said. "Lost puppy, library ghost, the talking umbrella, and the mango one without the throne."
"Let's keep three and try each on Monday," Kashish said, and they picked.

qa.q: How many ideas were on the chart paper?
qa.a: The chart paper had twenty ideas.

qa.q: How do you think Francis felt when Kashish wrote down the lost puppy idea without arguing?
qa.a: Francis probably felt encouraged and safe to keep sharing, since even the first idea went on the chart.

qa.q: Why was it better to judge the ideas only after the list was full?
qa.a: Because arguing early might have stopped people sharing, and waiting gave them twenty ideas to choose from before crossing any out.

qa.q: How might the rest of the class see the three skits on Monday?
qa.a: They may enjoy a better choice of skits, since the three were picked from many ideas and don't need too many props.

grounding: It shows children writing twenty skit ideas without arguing, then crossing out those needing too many props and keeping three to try.

subtype: Approach: generates a big list first and judges it afterwards [Action]
passage:
I'm Pallavi, and last month our group had to make a skit for Children's Day.
Afreen said, "Let's not fight this time. First we just write, then we choose."
So for ten minutes we wrote every idea on the back of old calendar pages. A dragon that is scared of mice. A school bus that talks. A girl who swaps places with her cat. Twenty ideas in total. Nobody said "that's stupid," not even when Rohit said "a dancing toothbrush."
Then we looked at each one and asked, can we do this with things from the classroom? The dragon needed a big costume. Out. The bus needed wheels. Out.
We kept three: the cat swap, the scared dragon without the costume, and the toothbrush. We tried them all on Friday.
The toothbrush won. I still can't believe it.

qa.q: On what did the group write their ideas?
qa.a: On the back of old calendar pages.

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel when the toothbrush idea won?
qa.a: Pallavi was surprised and amused, saying it still seems hard to believe. 😄

qa.q: What else could the group do next time to choose even faster?
qa.a: They could agree on the prop rule before writing, so they know how to judge as soon as the list is done.

qa.q: How might Rohit have felt when nobody laughed at the dancing toothbrush idea?
qa.a: Rohit may have felt safe and included, and later proud when that idea won.

grounding: It shows children writing twenty skit ideas before judging any, then crossing out those needing too many props and keeping three to try.
